title: Untold false news around COVID-19 circulated less on sina weibo than on twitter. How to overcome false information?
screen_reason: Content analysis of 1,923 tweets and 1,923 Sina Weibo posts captured with the keyword 'coronavirus' on 6-7 February 2020, each message coded by researchers into eight veracity categories. The paper reports the share of messages coded 'False news' on each platform (CONTENT) and the share of the corresponding retweets / Weibo reposts that were of false-news messages (SHARING), each with an explicit denominator in Table 2.

estimates.country: Not stated (international Twitter sample; keyword capture, no geographic restriction)
estimates.measure_type: % of retrieved coronavirus tweets coded as false news
estimates.denominator: 1,923 tweets containing the keyword 'coronavirus' published on 6-7 February 2020 (the most recently published tweets of each day, matched in number to the Weibo sample)
estimates.definition: Message coded in category 1 'False news': containing false information, including rumours, conspiracy ideas, myths, hoaxes, that are false and have a negative impact in the public sphere
estimates.misinfo_def: "False news: Tweets or Weibo posts containing false information, including rumours, conspiracy ideas, myths, hoa xes, etc., that are false and have a negative impact in the public sphere."
estimates.source_quote: Regarding RQ1, in the analyzed sample, 9,20% of tweets were coded as false news, before 3.69% of Weibo posts.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'False News Were Less Frequent and Less Shared On Weibo Than On Twitter' (p. 118); Table 2 (p. 118)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two researchers (a Chinese researcher plus European researchers with fact-checking expertise) coded every message in constant dialogue, comparing each message with its original publication and checking it against fact-checking tools (Fake News Detector, Maldito Bulo, Google Image, Tineye, InVID), scientific articles and WHO publications; a second review pass corrected mistakes. No kappa or other inter-coder reliability statistic reported ('dialogic reliability' instead).
estimates.moderator_quote: Criterion 2. Selection of the keyword. In this case, we have selected the keyword "coronavirus" for searching tweets and Weibo posts and capturing those messages.
estimates.notes: Two-day, single-keyword capture. denom_selection=curated because the tweet sample is a rank/time-truncated set ('choosing the same amount of Weibo posts starting with the last published tweets of the corresponding day'), not a random draw. The 1,923 denominator includes the 'Other' (40.77%) and 'Not valid' (16.43%) categories, even though the table footnote says those two categories were excluded 'for the analysis' - the reported 9.20% is computed on the full 1,923, as 177/1923 confirms.

estimates.notes: SHARING (content_share) because the denominator is the retweets the sampled tweets received, not the tweets themselves. The retweet denominator is very small (390 retweets across 1,923 tweets) and dominated by a handful of messages - the single most-retweeted false tweet drew 119 of the 204 false-news retweets - so the 52.31% is fragile; hence confidence=medium.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two researchers (a Chinese researcher plus European researchers with fact-checking expertise) coded every message in constant dialogue, comparing each message with its original publication and checking it against fact-checking tools (Fake News Detector, Maldito Bulo, Google Image, Tineye, InVID), scientific articles and WHO publications; a second review pass corrected mistakes. No kappa or other inter-coder reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Table 2. Frequency and percentage of retrieved messages (tweets and Weibo posts) and corresponding RT and WR*
estimates.notes: SHARING (content_share): denominator is the 31,009 reposts received, not the posts. Extremely skewed: 74.52% of all Weibo reposts come from a single 'Mixed' infographic that drew 22,971 reposts, which mechanically deflates every other category's share. confidence=medium for that reason.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The 'Mixed' category (partially true, partially false: 5.04% of Weibo posts, 1.51% of tweets; 74.52% of Weibo reposts, 7.18% of retweets) is a plausible broader-veracity variant, but the paper's own headline construct is 'False news' and any combined false+mixed figure would be a cross-category sum I computed, which R8 forbids; so no row. (2) The Discussion states 'the Twitter batch contained 5.51% more false news than Weibo batch' - a difference, not a share, so no row. (3) 'we found 1.72% more messages with scientific publications on Twitter than on Weibo' - same, a difference. (4) The science-based-evidence, fact-checking, facts and emerging-science shares are veracity categories of TRUE content, not misinformation, so not extracted. (5) The paper cites Fung et al. (2016) that 'only 2% of posts on Twitter and Sina Weibo contained Ebola-related misinformation' - a figure from elsewhere, excluded per R8. (6) The most-retweeted individual message counts (119 RT for the top false tweet, 14 reposts for the top false Weibo post, 66 RT / 94 reposts for the top science posts) are counts, not shares.

rob.design: Two-day (6-7 Feb 2020) keyword capture ('coronavirus') via the Twitter and Sina Weibo APIs using Python; 1,923 messages per platform (Weibo: 957 + 966, limited by what the Weibo web response returned, with unknown sampling/ranking; Twitter: matched N taken from the last published tweets of each day). Full-population coding of all 3,846 messages into an 8-category dialogic codebook by two researchers in constant dialogue, cross-checked against original publications, fact-checking tools (Fake News Detector, Maldito Bulo, Google Image, Tineye, InVID), scientific articles and WHO sources, with a second corrective review. Reliability reported only as qualitative 'dialogic reliability'; no kappa, no percentage agreement, no independent double-coding statistic. Authors flag the Weibo sampling opacity as the study's main limitation.
